title: Kinematics
tagline: Motion in a straight line and in a plane: position, velocity, acceleration, graphs, vectors, projectile motion and uniform circular motion.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Physics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Physics registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Kinematics is the description of motion without asking why the motion happens. That makes it the natural starting point for mechanics: before we talk about forces, we learn how to describe where an object is, how fast it is moving, and how its velocity is changing. This chapter deals with motion in a straight line first, then moves to motion in a plane, where vectors become essential. By the end, you should be able to read position-time and velocity-time graphs, use the equations for uniformly accelerated motion, and describe projectile motion and uniform circular motion in simple terms.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Position, displacement, speed and velocity; average and instantaneous quantities; acceleration; position-time and velocity-time graphs; uniformly accelerated motion; vectors and components; relative velocity; projectile motion; uniform circular motion

learningOutcomes: Distinguish distance from displacement and speed from velocity.
Use the equations for uniformly accelerated motion in one dimension.
Resolve vectors into components and add or subtract them.
Describe projectile motion and uniform circular motion in simple terms.

blocks.text: In one dimension, position can be represented by a single coordinate along a chosen axis. Displacement is the change in position, so it has a direction as well as a size. Distance, by contrast, is the total path length travelled. Speed is distance divided by time, while velocity is displacement divided by time. The difference can matter: a car that goes in a loop returns to its starting point, so its displacement is zero even though the distance travelled is not.

items: Displacement is a change in position; distance is the total path length.
Speed is distance per unit time; velocity is displacement per unit time.
Average velocity uses net displacement; average speed uses total distance.
Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a particular moment.

items.text: A particle moves from x = 0 m to x = 10 m in 2 s, then back to x = 4 m in the next 2 s. Its total distance is 16 m, so average speed is 4 m/s. Net displacement is 4 m over 4 s, so average velocity is 1 m/s in the positive direction.
items.note: The example shows that average speed and the magnitude of average velocity can differ even for the same journey.

learn.title: Graphs, acceleration and uniformly accelerated motion

blocks.text: Graphs are one of the best ways to reason about motion. On a position-time graph, the slope at a point gives the velocity. On a velocity-time graph, the slope gives the acceleration, and the signed area under the graph gives the displacement. When acceleration is constant, the results are the well-known equations of uniformly accelerated motion. These equations do not apply directly to non-uniform acceleration, so it is always worth asking whether the acceleration is constant before using them.

items: For constant acceleration, there are standard relations linking initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time and displacement.

items.text: If a velocity-time graph is a straight line sloping upward, the object is accelerating at a constant rate. If the same line slopes downward, the object is decelerating in the sense that its velocity is decreasing in the chosen direction.
items.note: A declining velocity line does not always mean the object is slowing down in an everyday sense; the sign depends on direction.

blocks.text: Many quantities in physics have direction, and those quantities are best handled with vectors. A vector has both magnitude and direction. When several motions or forces happen together, we often resolve each vector into components along convenient axes, work separately in each direction, and then recombine if needed. For two-dimensional motion, this is usually the most reliable way to avoid mistakes.

items: Components let us break a vector into simpler pieces along axes.
Vector addition is done component by component.
The direction of a vector matters; adding magnitudes without direction is usually wrong.

items.text: If a bird flies northeast, its motion can be separated into an eastward component and a northward component. The total displacement is not simply the sum of the two numbers as if they were lengths on the same line.
items.note: Resolving a vector is a tool for calculation, not a claim that the motion itself becomes one-dimensional.

learn.title: Projectile motion and uniform circular motion

blocks.text: Projectile motion is the motion of an object that is launched and then moves under gravity alone, ignoring air resistance in the simple model. In that model, the horizontal motion has constant velocity while the vertical motion has constant acceleration. Uniform circular motion is motion in a circle at constant speed. Even though the speed is constant, the direction is changing, so there is acceleration toward the centre of the circle.

items: Projectile motion: constant horizontal velocity, constant vertical acceleration.
The path of a projectile is parabolic in the simple model.
Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing direction.
The central acceleration in circular motion is due to the change in direction.

items.text: A ball thrown horizontally has no initial vertical velocity, but it gains vertical motion as it falls. Its horizontal progress continues at a steady rate, so the path curves downward.
items.note: The horizontal and vertical parts of projectile motion can be analysed separately in the simple model.

figures.caption: Figure: Velocity-time graph
figures.description: A straight-line velocity-time graph showing slope as acceleration and area as displacement.

keyPoints: Displacement has direction; distance does not.
Velocity is displacement per unit time; speed is distance per unit time.
On a position-time graph, slope is velocity; on a velocity-time graph, slope is acceleration and area is displacement.
The equations for uniformly accelerated motion apply when acceleration is constant.
In two dimensions, resolve vectors into components before combining them.
Projectile motion has constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration in the simple model.
In uniform circular motion the speed can be constant while the velocity changes because of direction.
examFocus: When a question asks for average speed or average velocity, decide first whether total distance or net displacement is needed.
Before using the uniformly accelerated motion equations, check that the acceleration is constant; those formulas are not generally true for varying acceleration.

vocabulary.meaning: The change in position of an object, including direction.
The rate of change of displacement.
The rate of change of velocity.
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction.
Motion of an object under gravity alone after it has been launched.
Motion in a circle at constant speed, with a continuously changing direction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is always true for a round trip that starts and ends at the same point?
questions.explanation: Displacement is the change in position; if the trip ends where it started, the displacement is zero even though the distance travelled may be large.

questions.prompt: On a velocity-time graph, the slope of the graph represents:
questions.explanation: The slope of a velocity-time graph gives the acceleration.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing slope with area, which gives displacement.

questions.prompt: A particle moves along a straight line with constant acceleration. Its initial velocity is 3 m/s and its acceleration is 2 m/s^2. What is its velocity after 4 s?
questions.explanation: For constant acceleration, final velocity = initial velocity + acceleration x time = 3 + 2 x 4 = 11 m/s.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting that acceleration is added each second, or mixing up the sign convention.

questions.prompt: In simple projectile motion, which quantity remains constant in the horizontal direction?
questions.answer: The horizontal velocity remains constant, if air resistance is ignored.
questions.explanation: In the simple model, there is no horizontal force, so the horizontal component of velocity does not change.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the horizontal speed also decreases like the vertical motion.

questions.prompt: A particle moves from x = 0 m to x = 20 m in 5 s, then reverses and moves to x = 5 m in the next 5 s. Find its average speed and its average velocity over the whole 10 s.
questions.answer: Total distance = 20 + 15 = 35 m, so average speed = 35/10 = 3.5 m/s. Net displacement = 5 m, so average velocity = 5/10 = 0.5 m/s.
questions.explanation: Average speed uses total distance; average velocity uses net displacement. The two numbers are different here because the particle turns back.
questions.commonMistake: Using the net displacement to calculate average speed, or forgetting to include the return distance.
